## Learning Objectives

By the end of today's session, you should be able to understand:

- how Quarto documents are structured
- how code and narrative work together
- how to render documents into polished outputs
- the foundations for reproducible research communication

::: notes
Key teaching goal: Communication and reproducibility, not memorization of syntax.
Many participants will remember concepts better than commands.
:::

::: notes
R4DS argues that communication is part of data science.

Data science is not:

Data → Analysis → Done

It is:

Data → Analysis → Communication → Impact
Lucky for you, this section focuses on the technial mechanics of Communication, not the act of conveying your thoughts and ideas to other people. That's up to you and your skills. 
How many of you have:

- copied a figure from R into PowerPoint?
- copied a table into Word?
- had to recreate a figure months later?
- struggled to remember how results were generated?
Spend 2-3 minutes discussing.
This creates buy-in for reproducibility.
Ask: "If nobody understands your work, did the analysis accomplish its goal?"
:::


# Chapter 28: Quarto

## Basics

**What is Quarto?**
A publishing system for creating reproducible documents by combining code, text, and visualizations.

**Every Quarto document contains four building blocks:**

- **YAML** – document settings (title, author, output)
- **Markdown** – narrative text
- **Code chunks** – R code that performs analyses
- **Rendered output** – tables, figures, and results

Example:

````markdown
```text
---
title: "Exercise Intervention Results"
author: "Morgan Brucks"
format: html
---

## Participant Characteristics

This report summarizes baseline demographics.
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
summary(demographics)
```
````



::: {.callout-note}
Think of Quarto as a recipe:

- YAML tells Quarto what to make.
- Markdown explains the story.
- Code performs the analysis.
- Rendering produces the finished document.
:::


## Editors

Quarto provides two ways to edit your documents: the Visual Editor for a word processor-like experience and the Source Editor for writing directly in Markdown. Both produce the same final document, so you can choose the workflow that best fits your needs.

**Visual**
<img src="https://r4ds.hadley.nz/quarto/quarto-visual-editor.png"/>


**Source**

````markdown
## Text formatting

*italic* **bold** ~~strikeout~~ `code`

superscript^2^ subscript~2~

[underline]{.underline} [small caps]{.smallcaps}

## Headings

# 1st Level Header

## 2nd Level Header

### 3rd Level Header

## Lists

-   Bulleted list item 1

-   Item 2

    -   Item 2a

    -   Item 2b

1.  Numbered list item 1

2.  Item 2.
    The numbers are incremented automatically in the output.

## Links and images

<http://example.com>

[linked phrase](http://example.com)

![optional caption text](quarto.png){fig-alt="Quarto logo and the word quarto spelled in small case letters"}

## Tables

| First Header | Second Header |
|--------------|---------------|
| Content Cell | Content Cell  |
| Content Cell | Content Cell  |
````

## Markdown vs. HTML

Both Markdown and HTML can be used to format Quarto documents. **Markdown is the preferred syntax for most writing tasks because it is concise, readable, and easy to maintain.** HTML is available when you need additional formatting or customization.

| Feature | Markdown | HTML |
|:--------|:---------|:-----|
| **Bold** | `**text**` | `<strong>text</strong>` |
| **Italic** | `*text*` | `<em>text</em>` |
| **Heading** | `## Heading` | `<h2>Heading</h2>` |
| **Bullet List** | `- Item` | `<ul><li>Item</li></ul>` |
| **Numbered List** | `1. Item` | `<ol><li>Item</li></ol>` |
| **Link** | `[Posit](https://posit.co)` | `<a href="https://posit.co">Posit</a>` |
| **Image** | `![Logo](logo.png)` | `<img src="logo.png">` |



**Example: Custom HTML Styling**

```html
<span style="color:#0055A4; font-weight:bold;">
Important Result
</span>
```

Markdown cannot easily apply custom colors or styles, but HTML can.


::: {.callout-note title="Hadley's Philosophy"}

**Use Markdown for almost everything.** It is easier to read, write, and collaborate on.

Use **HTML only when you need formatting that Markdown doesn't support**, such as custom styling, colors, layouts, or embedded web content.

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Take-Home Message"}

You do **not** need to learn HTML to be productive in Quarto. Markdown covers the vast majority of everyday writing tasks, while HTML is there when you need more control over the appearance of your document.

:::

## Code Chunks

Code chunks execute your analysis and insert the results directly into your document. Chunk labels and options help organize your work and control what appears in the final output.

**Chunk Labels**

Meaningful labels make documents easier to navigate and troubleshoot.

```{r}
#| echo: false

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(diamonds, aes(carat, price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1)
```

**Chunk Options**

Chunk options control **what your audience sees**, not what your code does.

| Option | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `echo: false` | Hide code, show results |
| `eval: false` | Show code, don't run it |
| `warning: false` | Hide warnings |
| `message: false` | Hide package messages |

Example:

```{r}
#| label: diamonds-summary
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

summary(diamonds)
```

**Global Options**

Instead of repeating options in every chunk, set them once at the beginning of your document.

```{r}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE
)
```

::: {.callout-note}
Chunk options affect a **single chunk**, while global options become the **default for every chunk** in the document.
:::

**Inline Code**

Inline code inserts **individual values** directly into your narrative.

Instead of typing:

> We enrolled **53940** participants.

Use:

```markdown
We enrolled `r nrow(diamonds)` participants.
```

which renders as:

> We enrolled **53940** participants.

Another example:

```markdown
The average diamond price was
`r scales::dollar(mean(diamonds$price))`.
```

renders as:

> The average diamond price was **$3,933**.

::: notes
**Why use inline code?**

If your data change, your text updates automatically the next time you render the document. This eliminates copy-and-paste errors and helps keep reports reproducible.

How many of you have ever updated a figure but forgotten to update the number in the paragraph above it?
Inline code solves exactly that problem.
:::

## Troubleshooting

Common errors include:

- missing package
- YAML spacing
- missing parentheses
- unclosed chunks

::: {.callout-tip}
Useful debugging advice includes:

1. Read the error
2. Find the line
3. Fix one thing
4. Render again
:::
